U.S. oil drilling accelerates gently - mostly in Texas

U.S. oil production has remained essentially flat over the last year and current prices are likely to encourage only modest growth in 2027.

Domestic producers are focused on controlling costs, disciplined investing and boosting returns to shareholders rather than growing output.

Stronger revenues stemming from the war with Iran and higher prices have been recycled to shareholders and used to pay down debt.

Price increases have not been large enough or expected to last long enough to produce a major response in terms of drilling and production.

But limited response does not mean no response at all. The rig count has been trending gradually higher with most of the extra units added in Texas ...

#Agriculture: Despite a welcome decline in global food prices last month, the UN FAO Food Price Index remained 5.9% above its year-earlier level, its fastest annual increase in more than a year. The index fell 1.6% in October, driven by lower prices for cereals, dairy and meat, while vegetable oils and particularly sugar continued to rise. Vegetable oil and sugar prices have emerged as a key source of food inflation, climbing 18% and 29% respectively over the past 12 months, highlighting the increasingly uneven price developments across major food categories.

Meanwhile, the Bloomberg Agriculture Commodity Index (BCOM) tumbled 8.7% in October as US harvest pressure, hopes for improved Black Sea exports and aggressive speculative long liquidation weighed on grain prices. The divergence between falling agricultural futures prices and still-elevated global food costs partly reflects differences in index composition. 

While the FAO index measures internationally traded food prices across five major categories, BCOM Agriculture tracks a narrower basket of commodity futures, making it more sensitive to developments in grains and speculative positioning. Processing, transportation and supply-chain costs can also influence how international commodity prices feed through to consumer food inflation.

Looking ahead, the strengthening El Niño event poses a growing upside risk, with potential weather-related disruptions to crop production across parts of Asia, Australia and South America threatening to reverse some of the recent declines. While near-term supply conditions remain relatively comfortable for several major crops, the risk of renewed food price inflation should not be dismissed.

#Commodities: Much can change before markets close tonight but so far the Bloomberg Commodity Total Return Index (BCOM TR) is heading for a weekly loss of around 4%, its worst since April 2025, trimming its year-to-date gain to 27% - still nearly four times the return delivered by the S&P 500. The setback follows a turbulent week in which a surprise US midterm election outcome sent shockwaves through parts of the US and global equity markets. Despite Friday's rebound, crude oil remains down around 12% on the week, while precious metals have recovered from their recent slump to post a 4.2% gain. Copper, meanwhile, is down 4.1% as the election result undermines expectations surrounding AI-driven demand and US import tariffs, while the agriculture sector has declined by around 3% with 11 out of 12 futures contracts suffering declines.

Brent has recovered strongly to trade around USD 100 after a week-long slump found support at the 200-day moving average near USD 93.55. The rebound reflects growing recognition that the recent selloff was driven more by hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough than concrete progress, with the path towards a US-Iran peace deal still long and fraught with obstacles. Iran, whose oil exports have slumped to near zero, is demanding an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets before agreeing to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. In the near term, attention remains firmly on Washington and how a politically weakened President Trump will respond following his midterm election defeat.

#Gold consolidates following strong short-covering rally: The pullback yesterday and during Asian trading today appears driven by broader risk aversion and profit-taking after CTAs and hedge funds completed an initial round of aggressive short covering. A rebound in oil prices, whose earlier slump helped trigger the rally, has added to the consolidation pressure. So far, the setback remains relatively shallow when measured against key Fibonacci retracement levels, and as long as gold holds above USD 3,975, we view the weakness as a correction following a strong rally rather than the start of a renewed downtrend. In the very short term, developments in US equities and, not least, President Trump's next moves regarding Iran remain the key drivers to watch. Meanwhile, lower Treasury yields and fading expectations of a December Fed rate hike continue to provide underlying support, partly offsetting renewed dollar strength.

Fed rate hike expectations continue to moderate, initially driven by the sharp decline in energy prices earlier this week and now by renewed weakness across the US technology sector. The combination has eased inflation concerns while raising questions about the resilience of economic growth, prompting traders to scale back expectations for further monetary tightening. 
December 2026 SOFR futures now imply less than one additional 25-basis-point rate hike, while December 2027 pricing points to a more gradual tightening path than anticipated at the September peak.
